argument: Peter Singer argues that because most people already believe inaction is wrong when a life is in danger right in front of them, and because people born into modern Western civilization have effectively 'won the lottery' of resources, that same moral obligation extends to the millions of preventable poverty deaths happening far away - inaction there is not morally different just because the suffering is distant. This is the basis of effective altruism: it's not enough to feel compassion and give; we should use reason to direct our giving - roughly 10% of income for most people - toward wherever it will do the most good, while still living sustainably enough to keep earning and giving over the long term.
keyIdeas: Almost everyone already believes that failing to help a dying child right in front of you is wrong, which sets up the question of why we treat distant, statistically massive suffering (millions of preventable child deaths a year) so differently.

The resources at your disposal change your moral culpability: having a shirt to sacrifice for a drowning person (or a lever to pull in the trolley problem) turns inaction into an actual moral choice you're responsible for, rather than simply being absent from the situation.

Effective altruism means using reason to find where money does the most good, not just giving generously to whatever cause is emotionally close (like a hometown church) - illustrated by Toby Ord, who shows that living comfortably and doing enormous good are not mutually exclusive.

Singer answers objections to a life of extreme self-denial with an oxygen-mask logic: being too depleted, unhealthy, or unable to function well undermines your actual capacity to keep earning and donating over time.

Effective giving requires research, not just trust in low administrative-overhead numbers - a charity spending more on operations can still do more lasting good than one that keeps overhead minimal - and small individual donations add up when many people give them, so Singer suggests redirecting the hedonic treadmill, the urge to earn more so you can buy more, toward earning more so you can give more.

terms.def: The approach, associated with Peter Singer, of using reason to direct charitable giving to wherever it will do the most measurable good, not just wherever feels emotionally compelling.
Singer's emphasis that good intentions aren't enough - donors must research and reason about which causes and charities actually produce the most good per dollar.
Singer's idea that how blameworthy inaction is depends on what resources (a shirt, a lever, money) a person actually had available to help.
The pattern of always chasing the next purchase for satisfaction that never lasts, which Singer suggests redirecting toward giving instead of spending.

The episode's own analogy: just like the airline instruction to 'secure your oxygen mask before you secure the mask of the child next to you,' staying fed, healthy, and professional first is necessary so you can keep earning and donating long-term.
